## Two points from the literature {#two-sentences-worth-keeping}

::: {.claimcard}
"the common single-path analyses in social and behavioural research should not be simply assumed to be robust to alternative analyses" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]
:::

::: {.claimcard}
A blueprint: precise question → causal reasoning (DAG) → multiverse → sensitivity analysis [@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial]
:::

::: {.small}
- Same-conclusion robustness and same-*number* robustness are different bars
- Justifiability is the criterion – choose with reasons, show the spread
:::

::: notes
The first point comes from the Multi100 paper: single-path analyses should not simply be assumed robust. And notice what preregistration did and did not do for you today. It protected your choice from being opportunistic, but it gave your preregistered dot no special status inside the curve. The preregistration made your one path defensible, and the grid showed that it was still one path among 840, so a report needs the preregistered path and the space around it together. From Auspurg and Brüderl comes the constructive recipe we followed – precise question, explicit assumptions, multiverse, sensitivity. And keep the two robustness standards apart in your own writing: same *conclusion*, which was seventy-four per cent in Multi100, and same *number*, which was thirty-four. When you claim robustness, say which one you mean.
:::

::: notes
There is no privileged single analytical path – only justifiable ones, explored openly. You have already done this once today: you made one defensible choice, you entered it and your reason in the preregistration block before running it, and you placed its result inside the space of alternatives. That habit transfers to any analysis you do, and the tooling, the estimand, the graph and the curve were all there to support it.
:::

::: notes
You take home a rendered report with a preregistration block in it, an estimand statement and a causal graph that you wrote for a real published claim, and two dots on the class chart, one exploratory from Task 4 and one preregistered from Task 5. The website on screen has everything else – the readings, the data, the companion modules, the specification-curve reading, and the full SCORE dossier on the paper if you want to dig further. Two pointers for keeping the habit alive wherever you work: most universities have a research-software engineering team and an open-research or library data service that run training like today's, and ReproducibiliTea journal clubs meet in dozens of cities – if there is not one near you, they will help you start one.
:::
